lede: A sixth and a fifteenth do not add until both are written in thirtieths. Algebraic fractions are the same, with one extra difficulty: you cannot see the common denominator until every denominator is factorised. After that the only hard part is the minus sign, which belongs to the whole of the numerator it is taking away.
can: Factorise every denominator and build the lowest common denominator from the distinct factors.
Bracket a subtracted numerator and change every sign inside it.
Factorise the collected numerator and cancel for the last mark.

md: This is the hardest algebra on the FM1 paper, and the examiners say so every year. Nearly everyone attempts it, most reach five marks out of seven, and very few reach all seven. One error does most of the damage: a product is subtracted and only its first term has its sign changed. The method is short. Everything that goes wrong goes wrong in two places: choosing the denominator, and handling the minus sign.

prompt: One tap to start, with numbers. What is the lowest common denominator of $\frac{1}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{15}$?
explain: Not 90. Six is $2 \times 3$ and fifteen is $3 \times 5$, so the three is used once: $2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30$. Algebraic fractions work in exactly the same way, with brackets instead of prime factors.

md: Factorise every denominator first. Then the lowest common denominator is the list of **distinct factors, each used once** — or more than once only if one denominator repeats it.

prompt: You are stuck on an add-or-subtract question. What is the first line you write?
answer: the lowest common denominator | the common denominator | the LCD | factorise the denominators | lowest common denominator | factorise the denominator
explain: Factorise the denominators, then write the lowest common denominator. It scores on its own and it makes the numerators obvious.

md: Multiplying the two denominators together always gives a common denominator, and when they share a factor it is not the lowest. The extra factor has to come out again at the end, and in the meantime the numerator has grown by a whole degree.

prompt: What is the lowest common denominator of $x^{2}-4$ and $x-2$?
explain: $x^{2}-4$ is $(x + 2)(x - 2)$, and $(x-2)$ is already one of those brackets. The other two options are the same common denominator written twice over, and both leave a fraction that still cancels.

md:
Once both fractions are over the same denominator, the numerators are combined. When you are **subtracting**, the whole of the second numerator is taken away, so it goes inside a bracket with the minus in front of it.
Then remove the bracket on the next line, changing the sign of **every** term inside. Doing it in two lines rather than one is what makes the difference, because the sign change is then something you do deliberately rather than something you remember.

explain: The product expands to $x^{2}-9$, and all of it is taken away. The second option changed the sign of the first term only, which is the pattern Summer 2025 examiners printed; the third added instead of subtracting.

md:
**1 Factorise every denominator.**
**2 Build the lowest common denominator** from the distinct factors.
**3 Multiply each numerator** by what its own denominator was missing, bracketing a subtracted one.
**4 Expand, apply the sign to every term, and collect.**
**5 Factorise the numerator and cancel.** Step 5 is the one that gets dropped when time is short, and it is usually worth the last mark.

prompt: Over $(x-2)(x+2)$, what does the numerator of $\dfrac{3}{x-2} - \dfrac{12}{x^{2}-4}$ become?
explain: The first numerator is multiplied by $(x+2)$ and the second is already over the full denominator, giving $3(x+2) - 12$. The second option forgot to multiply up; the third added instead of subtracting.

title: Adding and Subtracting Algebraic Fractions
why: The whole routine at writing speed, on the Further Maths shapes. Watch once, then answer the gate below without scrolling back.

explain: The numerator $3x-6$ factorises as $3(x-2)$, and $(x-2)$ cancels. The second option stops one line short; the third used the product of the two denominators.

md: The last mark is almost always for the cancel. So when the numerator is collected, try to factorise it — common factor first, then the quadratic — and check each factor against the denominator.

prompt: A numerator has come out as $3x^{2}-3x-18$ over $(x+2)(x+4)$. What do you do?
options: Leave it: a quadratic numerator cannot cancel with a product of brackets
explain: Dividing by 3 before factorising is the Summer 2019 error: it changes the expression. Factorise, cancel what matches, and the 3 stays where it is.

md: And when everything cancels, the answer really is a plain number. Summer 2025's question came down to a single value, and the report named candidates who stopped just short of it.

title: Adding Algebraic Fractions
why: A second pass with different shapes, useful once the method is familiar and you want speed.

prompt: You have reached $\frac{4x+12}{(x+4)(x-2)}$. What is left to do?
options: Take the common factor out of the numerator: $\frac{4(x+3)}{(x+4)(x-2)}$
answer: Take the common factor out of the numerator: $\frac{4(x+3)}{(x+4)(x-2)}$
explain: The numerator has a factor of 4. Nothing then cancels with the denominator, so that is the finished answer — but you only know by factorising and looking.

title: Summer 2025, FM1 Q7
md: Nearly all candidates attempted it and most scored five or more out of seven; very few reached full marks. The report lists the failures in order: the negative sign not applied across the bracket, brackets dropped altogether, premature cancelling across numerators and denominators, and stopping just short of the final value.

prompt: You are about to subtract a product of two brackets from another numerator. What do you write first?
options: A minus sign and then the whole product inside a bracket
The product expanded, with a minus in front of its first term
The two numerators side by side, to be collected later
answer: A minus sign and then the whole product inside a bracket
explain: Expand inside the bracket on the next line, and only then remove it. Two lines, and every sign changes together.

title: Why two denominators never cancel
md: Cancelling divides the whole top and the whole bottom of one fraction by the same thing. Two denominators belong to different fractions, so striking $(x-3)$ out of both divides neither fraction by anything: it simply changes both of their values.

prompt: In $\dfrac{x}{x^{2}-9} + \dfrac{2}{x-3}$, may the two $(x-3)$ brackets be cancelled against each other?
options: Yes, but only after the numerators are added
explain: Cancelling removes a factor of a numerator and a factor of the same fraction's denominator. Two denominators of different fractions never cancel each other.

md:
Factorise every denominator, then take each distinct factor once.
Multiply each numerator by what its own denominator was missing.
Bracket a subtracted numerator, then change every sign.
Factorise the collected numerator and cancel.

The **Express** wording, asking for one simplified fraction, ran at five marks; **Simplify fully**, with a combination and then a division, ran at seven. The marks follow the five moves, so every one is worth writing even if the next defeats you: the common denominator, the multiplied-up numerators, the collected numerator, the cancel. Stuck: factorise every denominator you can see and write the lowest common denominator down.
